Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 90, to amend the Canada Temperance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is simply to make applicable to districts within provinces under the Canada Temperance Act the provision which, under the Bill now in committee, is made for the protection of provinces in which there is a prohibitory iaw. The amendment suggested will make it an offence to send from a district within a province which is under the Canada Temperance Act, into any other part of the province, liquors to be used in violation of the law in force in the balance of the (province. It is to extend the same protection in the case of soiling liquor within territory covered by the Canada Temperance Act, where that is permitted, for the purpose of being sent beyond the limits of the province. Further than that, there is an amendment with regard to penalties, providing a maximum as well as a minimum penalty, and an amendment to correct an error in one section in which the word " municipality " was used where the word " county " or " city " should properly have been used.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Hon. A. E. KEMP (Acting Minister of Militia):
speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is in the

public interest that I should refer to a statement which was made in the Senate in reference to the recruiting of soldiers, particularly in the city of Toronto. According to the Senate Hansard report of the 12th of April, the Hon. Mr. Choquette made some very extraordinary statements in regard to the degeneracy of the soldiers, particularly those who are being recruited in the city of Toronto. The remarks would, however, apply to soldiers being recruited in any other part of Canada, as conditions are very similar in other places. The Senator referred to an item which he read from a newspaper, and on which he based part of his argument. That item is as follows:
The 169th Battalion, in recruiting to its strength of 1,131 men, examined 2,365 men, and therefore rejected as unfit 1,234. Another mounted squadron, amounting to 540 men, examined 1,744, and therefore rejected 1,204.
I shall not read what the Senator said, because his remarks have been published in the press, and we all know what they were. Later on he read to the hon. members	of the Senate, a letter
signed by a man who calls himself Robert Hazelton. The statements in this letter are extreme and uncalled for, and the whole letter can be judged by one remark in it. The writer refers to the Rev. Mr. Hincks in this way:
The "Rev." (?) Hincks is a faker. He is an adventurer' and to the native-horn he is known as a " Broncho Bullshooter," always blowing his own horn.
I desire to say that I am acquainted with the Rev. Mr. Hincks, as are many other hon. members of this Housb. He is a very highly respected clergyman, and is known as such from one end of this country to the other. Therefore, so far as the letter from Mr. Hazelton is concerned, it does not serve as a proper pretext for any of the remarks which Senator Choquette made.
I have received two telegrams from the commanding officer at Toronto, Brigadier General Loggie, which are as follows:
30,280 men have enlisted from Toronto. Officer Commanding 4th Canadian Mounted Rifles states that there were no rejections from the detail of Body Guard, Light Horse or 2nd Dragoons, hut 40 or 50 men in Brampton detachment were rejected for under-size. 169th reports that 1,336 rejections were made by his medical officer for chest measurements not being in proportion to height and age of men; flat feet and varicose veins. Medical examinations in this division were very strict and regulations absolutely adhhered to.
This causes an accumulation of men who have been previously rejected applying in each
succeeding unit in the hope of getting past the doctor. The recruiting depot is at work now on figures of total rejections in Toronto, and these will be forwarded early to-morrow morning (to-day). The A.D.M.S. of this division estimates about 30 per cent rejected. He found under-size, varicose veins and flat feet.
Further reference my telegram 13th instant, 37,402 recruits examined in Toronto, of which 7,122 rejected, 2,348 defective eye sight, 753 physically unfit, 626 flat feet, balance other defects.
Other defects include heart trouble, bronchitis, hernia, hammer toes, kidney disease, over age, and rheumatism.
Of these men rejected by 169th Battalion at least 25 per cent were repeated, that is men trying to enlist having previously been rejected. Total rejections of men examined 19 per cent.
I have here a short explanation which covers the whole matter, and which has been furnished to me by the officers of the department. It is as 'follows:
1.	The men to whom reference is made were not recruited and then rejected. They were medically examined before being recruited or enlisted, and upon being found not to be up to the medical standard, they were not taken on the strength and are not ,so shown.
2.	The medical standard required for enlistment is a high one, and it is in the Interest of the country that this should be so.
3.	In any large community, there are a number of mer. who are so anxious to enlist that they come up over and over again for enlistment in the hope of being able to pass the medical examination. Such men are known as " repeaters," and their anxiety to enlist is to their credit rather than otherwise.
4.	In England Lord Derby placed the deduction for medical unfitness at 40 per cent.
5 In Toronto 37,402 recruits have been examined of whom 7,122 have been rejected, or about 19 per cent. The cause of rejection being 2,348 for defective eye sight, and the balance for other defects, including over age, bronchitis, hernia, kidney disease and rheumatism, aa! also for minor defects such as flat feet or hammer toes and varicose veins.
6.	It is reported that the rejections for the Mounted Squadron were not as stated. The officer commanding the unit in question states that there were no rejections from the details received by him from the Governor General's Foot Guards, the Mississauga Light Horse or the 2nd Dragoons, and that only about 50 men were rejected by him for under-size.
7.	It is also reported that the rejections made by the medical officer for the 169th Battalion included at least 25 per cent of 'repeaters, i.e., men who tried to enlist but had previously been rejected. The other rejections were for failure to come up to the standard of chest measurement, for flat feet, varicose veins, etc.
8.	The percentage of rejections in Toronto is certainly not larger than in other parts of Canada or in any other country.
9.	It is absolutely false that there is any substantial proportion of men offering themselves for enlistment who are " diseased, depraved or deformed."
The city of Toronto has enlisted 30,280 soldiers. These men are as fine specimens

of manhood as the country can produce. They have offered their lives in a great cause. The blood of many of them has already drenched the plains of France to assist in crushing Prussian militarism, which seeks to dominate the whole world, including Canada. Many of them are now fighting side by side with soldiers of France who speak the same language as the hon. Senator. These men, who have been so foully slandered, are offering their lives with the soldiers of France to prevent the women and children of that nation from suffering horrors, tortures, and cruelties similar to those which a relentless foe perpetrated upon the women and children of poor, heart-broken Belgium. More than 300,000 men in Canada have offered their lives for the same purpose. Under these circumstances it is a fair question for me to ask, does Senator Choquette represent the opinion of any one in Canada except himself?

I think I would be in order, as a matter of privilege, to refer to the remarks made by the Acting Minister of Militia (Hon. A. E. Kemp) concerning the letter of one Robert Hazelton, which was mentioned in another part of this building. Coming from the constituency in which the writer of that letter lives, and having read the reflections he passed on those who were rejected when they applied for enlistment in Toronto, I have only this to say: that the constituency of South York, in which he lives, and which I represent, has sent over 3,000 enlisted men to the front, and the great bulk of them are British-born. I take this occasion to pay tribute to the loyalty and sacrifice of the British-born of Canada, and especially to those in my own riding, which has sent, along with the native-born, probably as fine a contingent, and certainly the greatest number of men sent from any riding represented in this House. On behalf of myself and of the constituency which I represent, I say that these remarks were unfair and most unjust, and a foul attack on the British-born in this country.

stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

I wish to refer very briefly to a discussion which took place in this House yesterday on the censorship of letters. I find it stated in Hansard that letters from the United States addressed to the Prime Minister and to the
ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux), had been opened and censored, and that a number of members bad received letters from internal points in the same condition. I may say that to-day I received a letter of a very confidential nature from a member of my own family, who is ill in an hospital in Boston, which had been opened and censored. I would like to ask the Postmaster General if he thinks it necessary that private letters, or any other correspondence, of a member of this House should be opened by the censors. If the members of the House of Commons cannot be trusted to carry on a loyal and patriotic correspondence, then the House of Commons had better be dissolved and the country run under some sort of autocratic form of government. I may be taking a pretty strong ground on this matter, but I desire to bring it as forcibly to the attention of the Postmaster General as possible, to see if he does not think that some instructions ought to be given to the censors to leave alone the private correspondence of members of the House of Commons.

I have a similar
complaint to make. I think it is very unfair that business letters coming from my own home town in Prince Edward Island should be opened and censored, -and letters of a confidential nature from the United States as well. I think we ought to have some ruling upon the matter.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I understood my hon. friend to say that letters addressed to him from Prince Edward Island had been censored. If so, would he kindly send over the envelopes,^ and I will attend to the matter immediately.
I will do so if I can find them.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: As to letters coming from, and going to, the United States, the rule is that all such letters are censored. The only exemption which has been made is in favour of consuls representing foreign countries. It is a great inconvenience, but it is a sacrifice which we are obliged to make in this time of war, and we have no discretion in the matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What about letters from one part of Canada to another?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Certainly they should not be censored. I have telegraphed and

telephoned all over the country, giving the strictest instructions to postmasters, and informing them that they would be held personally responsible for any error of that kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There never were instructions to censor letters addressed from one part of Canada to another.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
No, there were no
instructions to censor letters from any part of Canada to Ottawa, or to any other part of the Dominion. The only instructions issued were to censor mails which came from, or went to, the United States.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Then the
instructions were not followed.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: That is why I took the opportunity at once to repeat the instructions to the postmasters throughout the country, and to inform them that they would be held personally responsible for any such errors in the future.

speechtext: On the Orders of the DAY:

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. McCURDY (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext: I draw the attention of the Minister of Railways to a matter affecting a large number of employees on the Intercolonial railway. I understand that the scale of pay allowed to trackmen, ash-pit men, and that class of labour, has been $1.60 per day. In these days of much travel, when the railway is busy, and also in view of the conditions which prevail in the outside labour market, I would ask the Acting Minister of Railways if he cannot see his way clear to make a revision upward of that scale of pay?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Acting Minister of Railways):
speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: With reference to the question of labour on the Intercolonial and rates of pay, I may say that this matter was taken up by the Minister of Railways and Canals with the general manager as far back as February last, and my information is that last month the wages of trackmen were increased to $1.75 a day, on country sections, and to $1.85 a day in cities. It has also been decided, commencing on the 1st of April last, to pay the coal shovellers, ashpit men, etc., referred to by my hon. friend, at the rate of $1.70 per day. These advances have been made voluntarily by the minister and the general manager.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:
May I inquire when the return concerning small arms munitions will be laid on the Table?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am informed
that it has not yet been completed.

1 would ask the Acting Minister of Militia when I may expect the return moved for some time ago regarding the War Purchasing Commission. My hon. friend will remember that an order of this House was issued some three weeks ago, I think, for a return showing the transactions of the War Purchasing Commission down to the date of the order.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: My hon. friend may remember that on two or three occasions the Prime Minister explained to him the difficulty of getting that return prepared owing to the tremendous detail involved. If my hon. friend will look at his question and analyse it carefully, I think he will see that it is a very difficult return to prepare. I do not see how it is possible to get a sufficient number of clerks to prepare it. It would practically mean publishing the Auditor General's Report a year in advance, so far as the operations of the Militia Department are concerned. The operations of the Militia Department in connection with the War Purchasing Commission have been very extensive. About $63,000,000 have been spent by tfhe War Purchasing Commission on several thousand different items, as stated in an answer given to a question a day or two ago. I will submit to the House exhibits of the work of the War Purchasing Commission for the information of my hon. friend and of other members of the House, in order that they may be convinced of the difficulties of laying on the table of the House such a return as that asked for. I will bring these exhibits to the House at any time in order to demonstrate the impossibility of carrying out that order within any reasonable period of time, and I do not think that my bon. friend will insist on anything that is unreasonable.

There is nothing impossible, and surely the Government of Canada has enough money with which to hire clerks. This House has ordered that that return should .be brought down, and I see no reason why the House should not have it. Even if it does mean publishing the



Auditor General's Report a year ahead of time, surely it will do no harm to the people of Canada to get that important information. We are entitled to it if it does take some time and some money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will be brought down if it is possible, but work that is more important will not be put aside for it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: An order has been given by the House to have this report.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But the order
does not fix any particular time when it . is to be brought down. It will be brought down as soon as it is reasonably possible.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: After the session is over.
When it is of no value to us.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The House again in Committee on Bill No. 66, in aid of Provincial Legislation Prohibiting or Restricting the Sale or Use of Intoxicating Liquors.-Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice); Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
On section 4: accused must prove that he had good reason for believing liquor would not be dealt with illegally:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
There are three words
omitted from section 4 of the Bill which I desire to insert, although they do not alter the sense at all. As the section reads, it is only applicable to offences under section 1, but it is not clearly stated. The first line of the section speaks of a violation of this Act. The words left out are " of section 1."
I therefore move:
That section 4 be amended by inserting, in the first line thereof, after the word " violation," the words "of section 1."

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I have a copy of the Bill, but there are no such words in section 4.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
The Bill remained in
committee for the purpose of having it reprinted. It has been reprinted and I think it has been distributed. The Bill as originally introduced only created one offence which could come under this section, which is the section* dealing with the method of -proof. At that time it applied to any charge for a violation of this Act. Since then two

sections have been introduced; they have become sections 2 and 3, and the .section now .standing as section 4, that was left as applying to any violation of this Act, would apparently apply to an offence under one of the new sections, to which the context makes it perfectly clear that it could mot have any possible application.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: It was suggested the other day that the measure should prohibit the importation from one .province into another. In Ontario there are distillers and brewers. It was said in the legislature yesterday by the Provincial Secretary that they would have this anomaly, that distillers and brewers in Ontario could ship liquor, say to the province of Quebec, reimport it into Ontario, and sell it for personal use. Whilst in Ontario they would only ibe able to sell it to certain persons and in limited quantities, they might ship it to Quebec, bring it back, and sell it in unlimited quantities for personal use.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: If they did that they would be causing the liquor to be brought back from .outside the province of Ontario to be sold and used, and therefore they would be violating the statute. All these matters were thrashed out, and I tried to explain the situation when it was properly before the committee. The question now is whether these words should be inserted in section 4.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister of Justice what offence he refers to that section 4 would not be applicable to? It looks to me as if section 4 might very well be applied to subsection (a) of section 3-that is, the man who sends liquor in without labelling it. The burden of proof would be upon the party sending it in, or the defendant.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will just look at this section 4 he will see that the presumption that is created is a presumption that a man had knowledge that the goods were to be used in violation of the law of the province. That is all that section creates a presumption about, and therefore it could not find any application to the offence created by section 3, where the knowledge of any intended violation is not part of the offence. If there is objection to putting thesis words in I will drop them, because, even if the section stands as it is, it can only find application to an offence under section 1. But it is not quite correctly stated by being stated in the way in

which it is now. The presumption that is created would have no bearing upon the other offence, because it is a presumption in regard to knowledge that .the goods were going to be used in violation of the law, and that forms no part of the offences under sections 2 and 3.
Section, amended as proposed, agreed to.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I understood
there would be an opportunity of discussing fully every point of this Bill at this particular etage when -we have copies of the reprinted Bill before us. I am not sure whether I have misapprehended the meaning of section 3, tout dt strikes me that the offence under that section is practically the same as the offence under section 1, with the addition that the offender has sent in something that is not plainly labelled.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: That matter was fairly fully gone into, and I pointed out that this is the essential distinction between the two sections. Under section 1 the gist of the offence is that one sends liquor into the province with knowledge that it' is going to be dealt with in violation of the law of the province. No matter how many labels he puts on that liquor, he will toe guilty under that section if he does that. Under the other section, entirely without regard to what is the use that is going to toe made of the liquor, the man is required to put labels on, and he will be guilty of an offence if he does not label the liquor even though its purposs are the most legitimate conceivable.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I thank the minister for his explanation, but there is another point in connection with that. For an offence under section 3 there is no minimum penalty. I am rather inclined to think that in all legislation of this nature there should be a minimum penalty. The minister has recognized that in section 1. We have frequently found, in prosecuting cases of this kind before magistrates, who perhaps have not any very great experience in such matters, that their feelings have a good deal to do with the penalties. The minister has found it necessary in section 1 to provide a minimum penalty. Would it not be well to provide a minimum penalty in section 3 as well? If the minister does not approve of that, then let me make another suggestion. Should not a distinction be made between the first, second, and third offences, in section 3 as well as in section 1? It might 'be well for the minister to
follow out the policy he has laid down in section I, and apply it to section 3 in that particular.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Section 3 is a section which was asked for in the terms in which it is put in the Bill. However, I see no objection to inserting a minimum penalty. I am not so much impressed with the necessity of defining the penalty for subsequent offences, because the magistrate has the power to impose a penalty as high as $200. I do not know what the hon. member would suggest as a minimum penalty; I would suggest $50, and I would toe quite willing to insert that.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I do not think that would be amiss, but I think there should be a minimum penalty. Would the minister make any distinction between the first, second and subsequent offences?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I do not quite see the need of doing that in view of the nature of this offence.
On section 3, reconsidered:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I beg to move:
That section 3 be amended by adding the words " not less than $50 and " after the word " penalty " in the second line thereof.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I think it is quite right to have a minimum penalty, but I do not see why it should be less than the minimum in the first section. It seems really to be a worse offence to put a fictitious label on a parcel than to send a parcel in : the former is an aggravation of the latter offence, and why we should, make a minimum penalty of $200 in the first section and of $50 in this section does not appear clear.
Section, amended as proposed, agreed to.
On the preamble:

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Section 5 says:
The court shall take judicial notice of the statutes and law of the province into which intoxicating liquor has been or is alleged to have been shipped, taken, brought, carried or imported contrary to the provisions of this Act.
Does the minister think that this will include legal procedure also?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
That section has been adopted just as it stands; it has not- been altered in any way in the reprinting, but I have no objection to answering the question in regard to it. Inasmuch as a prosecution may take place in a province other than the province into which the liquor is

sent, it occurred to us-and I think it would be true-that a magistrate sitting in that province would not be called upon without this disposition, to take cognizance, judicially of the statute of the province into which the liquor was sent, and part of the provision is that it should be sent with intent to violate. This section is inserted to obviate the necessity of bringing witnesses to prove what the law of the province is, in order that a man may be able to produce the statute and .say: That is the law of the province, and the magistrate will take cognizance of it.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: There is no provision for appeals.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The prosecution: is by summary proceeding, and the provisions of Part 15 of the Criminal Code will apply so far as appeals are concerned.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Would it not be better to state so in the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I really do not see that we gain anything, because we have made this an offence punishable upon summary conviction, and we have a statute expressly made for determining all those matters with regard to offences punishable upon summary conviction.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) was asking why the minimum penalty under section 3 is lower than that under section 1. I might give a little explanation. A man might be charged on one charge with the two offences. The gist of the offence under section 1, as I understand the minister, is the sending in of liquor to be used contrary to the law of the province, whereas the gist of section 3 is the false marking.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I think a man might be charged on both counts. As regards making the minimum penalty under section 3 smaller than that under section 1, there are circumstances in which an offence under section 3 might be very serious; but a man might be guilty of the offence of failing to put a label on under conditions that might make it a very trivial offence, and I think we might leave the penalty to the discretion of the court.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Does the minister not think it might be preferable to apply the provisions of the Canada Temperance Act with regard to procedure and appeals to applying the Criminal Code, because in the Canada Temperance Act the tribunal is

expressly defined, and the Court of Appeals is also expressly defined?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will find that the same things are expressly defined in the part of the Criminal Code to which I have referred with regard to offences punishable upon summary conviction, and now that we have made this an offence punishable by summary conviction, it seems to me that it is more desirable that we should make it come under the general law governing such offences. The provisions of the Canada Temperance Act are direct prohibitory provisions made by this Parliament, and dealing with the actual sale and trafficking in _ liquor directly. Here we have special legislation creating a new offence susceptible of being dealt with upon summary conviction, and I think that the hon. gentleman, if he will look up the provisions of part 15 of the Criminal Code, will find that they are as satisfactory .as the other, and we avoid making this particular offence, which is an offence to be dealt with upon summary conviction, differ from all other offences of the same class.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Is there any time limit affecting prosecutions under this legislation? Under the Canada Temperance Act a man must be prosecuted within three months of the committing of the offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I am not prepared to say offhand, without the Act before me, whether there is any general provision in the Criminal Code applicable ,to offences of this kind prescribing the time during which prosecutions may be brought. My impression is that there is one. If there be none, we are not by this 'legislation fixing any special time during which the prosecution must he brought.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Last year and the year be-fpre, on taking up the Naval Service Estimates, the right hon. leader of the Opposition requested me to make a general statement of the affairs of the Naval Service. So, before taking up the different items separately, I might read a memorandum I have prepared regarding this activities of tiie Naval 'Service with relation to the war:
Activities of the Naval Service Department in relation to the War.
Prior to the outbreak of war, preparations were made to meet all contingencies which could be foreseen. When war appeared imminent, it was only necessary to carry out or expand these preparations. Orders in Council which it would be necessary to pass had been prepared beforehand. Inter-action between the Naval and other departments in connection with war activities had been thought out, and the procedure to be adopted, the responsibility for taking the necessary action, and the methods to be employed in so doing had all been arranged so far as such matters could be foreseen. Thanks to the forethought which had been expended these directions, there was much less friction and delay in many important matters than might have been expected and anticipated.
In addition to the general administration of the dockyards at Halifax and Esquimau, the Naval College, at Halifax, the Niobe, Rainbow, Shearwater and submarines, Fisheries Protection Service, Rife Saving Service, Fisheries, Tidal and Currents Survey, Radiotelegraph and Hydrographic Survey, the department is actively employed on such matters as naval intelligence, contraband, enemy and neutral commerce, censorship, movements, etc., of store and troop transports, as well as being responsible for and organizing mine-sweeping flotillas, coastal patrols, harbour defence, etc., etc.
In order to cope with the greatly increased work thrown upon the department, it has been necessary largely to increase the staff employed at headquarters. Leaving out such sections of the department as Hydrographic Survey, Tidal and Currents Survey, Fisheries, etc., which have not been much affected by the war, the staff employed has been increased by over 100 per cent.

As an instance of the great amount of work got through in the department, one entirely new section alone, the Intelligence Branch, which has been organized since the outbreak of war, and in which only 12 per cent of the personnel of the staff of the department are employed, during February of the present year, received 972 letters, memoranda and reports, and 949 telegrams, whilst it despatched 1,476 letters and 726 telegrams. The work of the other branches has been "Correspondingly increased.
On the declaration of war the Niob* hnd Rainbow and the officers and men serving in them were placed at the disposal of the Admiralty. At that time the Rainbow was in full commission, having been in all respects prepared for sea shortly before, in order to carry out patrol duty on the Behring sea. The British Government asked us to undertake that work in connection with the treaty in regard to pelagic sealing. She was therefore available for immediate service, and was at once despatched south from Esquimalt to guard the trade routes and protect the sloops Algerine and Shearwater which were proceeding north. These two vessels arrived safely at Esquimalt, and since that time the Rainbow has bean continuously employed in the protection of trade and other duties in the North Pacific and on the coast of British Columbia, being attached to a squadron under the orders of the imperial senior officer at that station.
Arrangements were immediately made to commission the Niobe, and to complete her crew to full sea-going requirements. This was done partly by the transfer of the Imperial officers and men of the Algerine and Shearwater, which, owing to their small fighting value, had been ordered by the Admiralty to pay off at Esquimalt, and partly by the inclusion of 100 Newfoundland naval reserve men, the remainder of the crew, to the number of about 400, being recruited from men who had served in the British Navy and were resident in the Dominion. A large number of men of this class volunteered their services. As many as necessary were entered for service during the period of the war.
As soon as she was ready, the Nioble joined the squadron under the command of the Rear Admiral commanding the North American Station, in which she did duty until September last, when, owing to the very considerable amount of almost continuous steaming she had done since the outbreak of the war it was considered that the general state of her machinery and boilers did not warrant her continuance in this duty. This being the case, in conjunction with the urgent necessity of a depot ship to be used to accommodate the numerous drafts of men passing through Halifax, and of a parent ship for the vessels employed on patrol work, etc., on the Atlantic coast, it was decided to pay her off and re-commission her for the purposes indicated. Since that date she has proved very suitable for her new functions, and has been of utility in connection with Canadian and Imperial service.	,
The crews of the two submarines which were purchased by the Dominion Government at the outbreak of war, were recruited from officers and men in the Dominion, the Government being fortunate in this respect in obtaining the services of two retired officers of the Royal Navy who had both had several years' experience in submarines. These vessels were also placed at the disposal of the Admiralty.

Permission was also obtained from the Admiralty to use the Shearwater as a mother shin for. the submarines. This vessel was therefore adapted as necessary for this duty, and has proved her suitability for it. The Shearwater and the two submarines have been actively employed in the defence of the British Columbian coast, and, since the removal of the menace of Admiral von Spee's squadron, have continued training operations and cruises.
Naval depots were established at Halifax and Esquimalt for the accommodation of supernumerary ratings, etc. At Halifax buildings in the dockyard were adapted and utilized until it became necessary, owing to the increase in number and size of drafts, and other conditions, to utilize the Niobe for this purpose, as already explained.
At Esquimalt the depot was used for the training of R.N.C.V.R. officers and men.
A large number of other vessels, both Governmental and private, are being used in connection with the naval defence of the coast. They are being employed on the various services hereinafter specified.
The ice-breaker Earl Grey, on her sale to the Russian Government, was transferred to this department to be sent to Archangel; a crew of naval ratings was provided, and the vessel v:< s successfully navigated to her destination, the voyage of 3,000 miles being completed in 14 days. On arrival at Archangel she was turned over to the Russian authorities. The crew returned by ordinary steamer, some rejoining the British Navy, and some returning to Canada for further services in the Canadian Navy.
Personnel.-On the outbreak of war, recruiting was actively carried on to complete the Niobe's crew, as previously stated, and to obtain the requisite crews for other vessels employed on subsidiary duties, preference being given to men with previous naval experience. The naval volunteers which were established just previous to the outbreak of war developed largely in the west, where some 400 officers and men are enrolled. These volunteers have done good service both ashore and afloat, a considerable number having served con-4 p.m. tinuously in the Rainbow since the outbreak of hostilities, whilst others are in H.M.S. Newcastle, the various vessels at Esquimalt, including the submarines and their parent ship the Shearwater, and about 100 have been transferred to the Atlantic coast for duty in the various patrol vessels, etc., employed there. Their training is being continuously carried on.
The department has acted as recruiting agent for the Admiralty, and a large number of Imperial service officers and men have been reached, and arrangements made for their transportation from all parts of the Dominion to England. The department has also handled the transportation arrangements for numerous drafts of naval ratings proceeding to and from England.
In April of last year the Admiralty requested the department to select a considerable number of men to be trained as pilots for the Royal Naval Air Service. This involved a very considerable amount of work and correspondence, many hundred of applications for entry being received from all over the Dominion. These had to be gone into individually and arrangements made for the interviewing and medical examination of likely applicants. The number called for by the Admiralty was twice increased, but the full quota was easily obtained,

and nearly all have now obtained their flying certificates and have been sent to England. At the present date 180 have left Canada and are either on active service or completing their training in England prior to going on active service.
Recently the department was also requested by the Admiralty to ascertain what men could be entered for the Auxiliary Motor Boat Patrol Service. Several hundred applications have been received, and these are being classified pending the arrival of an officer, who, it is understood, is coming from England to make final selections.
Mine-sweeping.-At certain ports a minesweeping flotilla is provided. This consists of comparatively small vessels whose duty it is to keep the approaches to the harbour clear of enemy's mines. This entails daily operations on their part.
Patrol.-A number of vessels are employed on patrol duty on different parts of the coast. They are charged with the duty of keeping watch for hostile craft of all sorts, and tracing rumours of their presence. The patrol is organized jointly with the Imperial authorities and the Government of Newfoundland.
Wireless telegraphy and censorship.-It was found necessary at the beginning of the war to close a large number of stations. On the west coast, the situation having now relaxed, they have all been re-opened. In conformity with the procedure in other parts of the Empire, a censorship is imposed on all wireless telegraph messages emanating therefrom.
Enemy and neutral commerce.-All enemy merchant ships were ordered to be detained on the outbreak of war, the arrangement for this being concluded with the Customs Department.
The only German ship in Canadian harbours was the barque Bellas which was seized at Ri-mouski and has since been condemned in the Prize Court.
The Austrian steamer Ida was seized also, but subsequently released under the " days of grace " allowed.
Many important questions regarding contraband and neutral commerce are continually arising which indirectly affect the department and are dealt with accordingly.
The department is continually in conference with the Customs Department with a view to preventing coal or supplies reaching tne enemy or enemy agents by means of neutral or other vessels. Stringent steps have been taken to this end.
Coast defences.-At certain places guns have been mounted and manned by naval officers and men, whilst in other places protection has been prepared by the provision of motor torpedo boats and mines prepared for laying in case of emergency. As the situation relaxed, these were gradually withdrawn.
Naval intelligence.-A system for the collection and distribution of naval intelligence has been organized, acting in concert with the Imperial authorities.
Harbour defence.-All details connected with naval defence at defended ports are undertaken by this department. Amongst other things at Halifax and Quebec an examination service was instituted before the outbreak of war and has been uninterruptedly continued, except at Quebec, during the winter season. This is for the purpose of insuring that no vessel with hostile intent shall enter the harbour, and also to facilitate the ordinary flow of commercial ships.
To this end every vessel entering the harbour is boarded outside the port and her papers, crew, etc., examined. If satisfactory, she is allowed to proceed; otherwise, she is detained for further examination.
With respect to the naval dockyards, both establishments have been worked to the full output, a considerable amount of overtime having been worked. Halifax is being used as the base for vessels of the North Atlantic Fleet which has been lately strengthened; the dockyard is being used for carrying out repairs to these vessels and keeping them in going order. Number 4 jetty has been repaired and lengthened so that it will now accommodate large ships. The Niobe has been fitted up as a very efficient receiving ship. At the Esquimau yard the expenditure and personnel have risen correspondingly and work has been carried out on Imperial and Allied vessels, as well as those of the Canadian service. The total amount of money paid per month in wages for the two yards is approximately 300 per cent more than that customary to be paid for the same period prior to the war.
Stores and Contract Branch.
The activities of this branch have been maintained and considerably augmented during this year both at headquarters and at the dockyards at Halifax and Esquimau, and elsewhere as necessary.
Supplies are still being procured with difficulty and at greatly enhanced prices. The domestic market is uncertain, especially as regards metals and textiles. Nevertheless, reserves have been well maintained and, where necessary, increased. The value of stock available for immediate issue at the end of February was in excess of $600,000, and issues up to that time exceeded $750,000. (Note A.)
Purchases aggregating in value over $1,200,000 have been made. These include provisions, clothing, medical supplies, naval stores of every description, fuel, ordnance stores and ammunitions, etc. (Note B.)
Arrangements have been maintained on both the east and west coasts for the supply of fresh provisions at short notice to all ships requiring such, both Canadian and Imperial.
In addition, material assistance is being rendered to the Imperial service in the supply of stores of every description to His Majesty's ships from the several dockyards and also by direct purchase. Considerable quantities have also been supplied to and purchased for Bermuda dockyard.
Assistance has also been rendered in the same manner, but in lesser degree, to the Japanese, Russian, and French Governments, as well as to the Commonwealth of Australia. (Note C.)
The Imperial authorities continue to utilize our facilities at both dockyards to keep in reserve large supplies of special stores for the use of ships doing duty in the North Atlantic and in the Pacific. These are accounted for and looked after in the same manner and with the same care as are Canadian stores. Ordnance stores and ammunition particularly require great care and it has been found necessary to organize special depots for the purpose.
Supplies of fuel have been well maintained on both coasts. Receipts at Halifax exceeded 65,000 tons and at Esquimau 25,000 tons. Issues at Halifax exceeded 70,000 tons and at Esquimau 30,000. Balance of stocks have been somewhat reduced, but are still sufficient for all purposes and are constantly being replenished.

In addition to fuel handled at the dockyards, over 65,000 tons of Canadian coal was purchased for delivery direct to ships, of which over 50,000 tons was for the Imperial service. (Note D.)
During the year three small ships were added to the permanent establishment by purchase, and three others were added for the period of the war, two of which were loaned by private individuals and the other by the Department of Customs.	'
These were all thoroughly equipped and stored and are being served regularly.
In addition, 18 vessels of varying dimensions have been chartered for various purposes on the Atlantic Coast, such as mine-sweeping, harbour defence, examination service, and patrol work. Also 14 large motor launches have been chartered for patrol service in the gulf of St. Lawrence and adjacent waters, and 5 for service on the Pacific Coast.
Supply depots have been provided as necessary at points along the coast for the convenience of these vessels.
H.M.C.S. Rainbow has been maintained in commission and kept fully stored and equipped for any emergency.
Canadian Trnsportation.
The arrangements under which the Canadian Transport Service operates have been continued in force and considerably enlarged. There are nOw operating under Admiralty Charter on this service over sixty ships. The work incidental to handling this service is carried out under the joint direction of the Acting Director Overseas Transport, who is responsible for the organizing of the cargo, and the Department of the Naval Service which directs the movements of the ships and is the medium of communication with the Admiralty on all matters.
Up to the close of navigation at Montreal last fall over 300,000 tons of freight had been handled by this service and since then export tonnage has greatly increased. In the month of February 138,000 tons were shipped from the ports of Halifax and St. John. In March 173,000 tons. The number of steamers handled at these ports .during these two months was fifty -six. Arrangements have been made for the loading and despatch during the summer season of navigation of an average of one ship per diem.
In addition to the general stores handled by this service over forty cargoes of timber, aggregating about one hundred and twenty-five million feet, board measure, have been shipped from various ports on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.	<
Radiotelegraph Branch.
The policy of the Government in developing and maintaining an efficient Radiotelegraph Service, and its early recognition of the fundamental principle of absolute Government control of all wireless matters, has amply justified itself in the present emergency.
It is hardly necessary for me to emphasize the vitally important part this comparatively new medium of communication is playing in the present war, and, I am pleased to say that our policy of preparedness in this regard is a tribute to the foresight of the officials in whose hands has been the organization of this service.
Its most important object is, of course, to provide efficient and adequate means of communication with such fleets as may be operating in our waters. Our stations, owing to the geographical position of this country, occupy a

natural strategic position with regard to the North Atlantic and Pacific oceans, and by the reservation of certain stations solely for naval work, and the concentration of the best operators in the country at those stations, we are providing a service which is meeting, in the highest sense, the present requirements of the Admiralty.
Radiotelegraphy, I might add, is also of inestimable value in providing a means of communication with points otherwise inaccessible except by cable, thus Canada, possessing as it does two transatlantic stations, is to a certain extent independent of the cables, and, in case of interruption, would by no means be isolated from the Mother Country.
It would not, at this moment, be wise to make public full details of what has been done in connection with our service since August 1914, but I may say, that, immediately hostilities became imminent, a pre-arranged war scheme was placed into effect. With the exception of the Mabconi transatlantic station at Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, all the licensed stations throughout the Dominion were closed down, 108 in all, and arrangements were made with the Dominion police and militia authorities to see that no unauthorized stations were established ; 20 Government stations not absolutely essential to war procedure, and which it was impossible to adequately guard, were also closed until the situation modified itself, when 17 of them were reopened for commercial or naval work. The stalls of the Government stations left open were augmented, and certain other stations, operated by the Marconi Company under contract, were taken over by the department and provided with a naval staff. The Militia Department provided military guards at all the important stations, and censor staffs at such stations as were permitted to handle commercial messages.
The transatlantic station at Newcastle, N.B., having a staff of foreigners, was, naturally, a matter of suspicion to the department; a small military detachment was accordingly immediately detailed to assume possession. This station remained closed until August 19, 1914, on which date an officer of this department was detailed to act as censor and technical assistant to the military officer commanding, and the station was permitted to resume operations. It has since been found advisable to increase the naval staff, and this department has assumed control of the operation of the station.
A certain amount of work in connection with new construction, and the enlargement of existing stations has also been undertaken. All the vessels of the Patrol Fleet have been equipped with wireless apparatus and, under an arrangement with the Admiralty, the department is installing and operating radio equipments on all unequipped munition transports plying to Canadian ports. All told, 45 ship sets have been installed to date. The operators are enlisted in the R.N.C.V.R., but, owing to the shortage of competent men, it has been necessary to hire 20 from the Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company for duty on transports; these will be replaced by R.N.C.V.R. ranks as they become available. All operators on ships and shore in the employ of the service are entered in the R.N.C.V.R. with the rank of " wireless operator," equal to that of 4' non-executive warrant of ficer," a total of 84 men not including the technical and executive staffs.
The regular work of the stations has, as far as possible, been carried on in addition to the extra duties entailed by the war, and last year,

in spite of the closing of many of the stations the total number of words handled amounted to 3,055,543.
In conclusion let me state that the war has demonstrated beyond mistake the wisdom of the attitude of the Canadian Government, past and present towards the valuable discovery of radi otelegraphy.
I thought that it would be well, perhaps, to make a general statement along these lines before taking up the items in the Estimates.
I think my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) desired to know what amount we had spent last year.
