I am sorry my hon.
friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), the former Minister Of Naval Affairs, is not present, as he would have been able to speak with reference to these Estimates to greater advantage than I can. I desire to express my appreciation of the fact that the minister, referring to the value of the radiotelegraph service, thought that both this Government and the previous Government were to be congratulated upon the acquisition and development of that service. It is a very important service, but I thought it was quite a serious omission in the statement of my hon. friend that, when he was in the mood to congratulate the Government, he did not go a little further and congratulate the Government and Canada upon the fact that the late Government had acquired two very worthy war vessels

which had proved of great service to Canada for the defence of her coasts since the outbreak of the war. Perhaps that was an omission on the part of my hon. friend that was somewhat pardonable under the circumstances, and with the recollection that he would have of what has taken place in connection with the Canadian naval service in recent years. I have had the opportunity of reading the report of ViceAdmiral Kingsmill for the year ended the 31st March, 1915, and I have observed that in that report he said:
With regard to the activities of the Naval Service Department in relation to the war, preparations having previously been made to meet all contingencies which could be foreseen, it was only necessary to carry out or expand these preparations when war appeared imminent.
That seems to me a somewhat extraordinary statement to make, in view of the fact that the Niobe, so far from being kept in a state of preparedness to meet any eventualities which might occur, was actually laid up at Halifax and had her boilers stuffed with some sort of material which would prevent them from rusting; so that it took several weeks before the Niobe could be got ready for sea after the war broke out. It did strike me that that was a strange way to have a vessel in commission. That is the Government's way of keeping a war vessel in commission, and it may be a way which commends itself to the Naval Service Department under its present management.
I do not wish to unduly criticize that proceeding, but it may be thought desirable 'to have some further explanation as tc whether this is a mode which should generally be adopted when it is felt desirable to make preparation in the event of war.
In regard to the Rainbow, there is no doubt she was kept in commission, but apparently not because the gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches really thought that war was imminent, but because the British Government had requested that the Rainbow be used in patrolling the Behring sea. It is most fortunate that the British Government thought that Behring sea ought to be patrolled, because I have no doubt that the boilers of the Rainbow would have been choked up with this non-rusting material with which the Nioibe was so plentifuly supplied, and which took some weeks to remove in order to have the latter -vessel placed in commission. Vice-Admiral Kingamill bears testimony to the value which the Rainbow has been to Can-

ada for the defence of the Pacific coast. He says:
The Dominion Government shortly before the outbreak of war purchased two submarines which were building at Seattle for the Chilean Government. The crews were recruited from officers and men in the Dominion, the Government being fortunate in this respect in obtaining the service of two retired officers of the Royal Navy who had previous experienec in submarines. These vessels also were placed at the dispsal of the Admiralty.
Permission was also obtained from the Admiralty to use the Shearwater as a depot ship for the submarines.
These three vessels have all been actively employed in the defence of the British Columbia coast.
Thus bearing testimony to the value which this much-despised Rainbow has been to Canada for the defence of the Pacific coast.
As to the submarines, I do. not propose to say anything now, but I realize that it i3 important to have submarines for the defence of the coasts of Canada. Without going into the past, without sayipg anything that might lead to altercation or unpleasantness, I wish to express the hope that even at this late date my hon. friend will see his way clear to engage in the building of small war vessels at all events, to be placed in the service of the Canadian Government. It is a matter that ought to be remarked upon that the only submarines which have been built in Canada since the war broke out have been built at the shipbuilding plant of the Canadian Vickers-Maxim Company, a plant which, I am proud to say, I as Minister of Public Works, was instrumental in having established in Canada. My hon. friend may perhaps remember-I am sure he will not object to my calling his attention to the fact-that on one occasion in this Parliament he spoke of a company whose plant I had visited-that of the Fore River Shipbuilding Company, a most magnificent plant, which at that time was only in operation for a year or two, and which had turned out a large number of war vessels, submarines, cruisers, and commercial vessels for the Government of the United States-he spoke of it as a bankrupt concern. Instead of orders being given direct to Canada for the building of submarines, this company, I think my hon. friend has knowledge now, has received an order for the building of twenty submarines from the British Government, the contract price being some $10,000,000. Fortunately, owing to the fact that under international law the sending away of these submarines,

when they were completed, from the United States to one of the belligerent countries would not be permitted, an order was given for half of them to be built at the plant of the Canadian Vickers-Maxim Company, near Montreal. In that way a considerable amount of labour was employed in Canada. I believe that these submarines, after having been taken across the Atlantic, did exceedingly good service in connection with the1 British fleet. I am told that one of these submarines built in Canada sank a German cruiser in the Black sea, showing certainly that it was a most efficient vessel.
It is a matter of regret to me also to learn that this Government, instead of engaging in the building of patrol boats and establishing shipyards on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, has purchased vessels of this character. I am told that three of these vessels have been purchased in the United States. The minister will correct me if I am wrong.
The minister has also stated that nineteen motor boats were chartered for use by the Canadian Government. If there is one class of boats which Canada could build, and with very little delay, it is motor boats. There is no reason in the world why motor boats for the service of Canada, as well as motor boats for the service of the Imperial Government, should not be built in Canada. May I appeal to my hon. friend to take time by the forelock, to look ahead, not to be guided by what he may toe absolutely certain will happen, tout toy what may by possibility toe required for the defence of Canada, and let him encourage the building, not of large war vessels, but of submarines, motor boats, oil-tank vessels, cruisers, and torpedo boat destroyers, in Canadian shipyards. Let him give reasonable encouragement to this, and he will be doing what may in the future prove to be of inestimable value for the defence of Canada and for the service of the Empire. We cannot be sure how long this war may last. When it broke out there were many gentlemen in this House, even gentlemen occupying seats upon the treasury benches, who thought it would toe a light task to defeat Germany, and who enjoined our young men to come upon a holiday trip to Berlin. That was the idea which many of them had. My hon. friend from North Simooe (Mr. Currie) said the other day that when he crossed he supposed the war w'o-uld last about six weeks. Well, it has lasted now twenty months, and no man who looks at the question seriously can
predict with any degree of confidence that it may not yet last for just as long a time as it has already done. Therefore it seems to me that this Government ought to become sensed of the responsibility which rests upon this Dominion as one of the great overseas Dominions of the Empire, and it ought to avail itself of the opportunity which Canada presents for building ships upon tooth oceans, and enter at once upon the building of those smaller war vessels which I have mentioned. In doing that the Government might also at the same time encourage the building of a Canadian mercantile marine* to assist in carrying on the trade of Canada. Yesterday, when my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) had his Estimates under consideration, I ventured, because I feel deeply upon this question, to attack the Government because, although this Parliament has been in session for three months, and although we have had two sessions since the war broke out, the Government has not taken one effective step to encourage the building up of a Canadian mercantile marine. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce asked me to wait a while, not to disturb him in getting his Estimates through;	but	now, when	we	are	discussing	the	Estimates	of	the	department whose minister ought to be giving special attention to this subject, I venture to suggest the matter again for the consideration of the Government. I feel sure that gentlemen on both sides of the House will let this Government know what they think o.f the lamentable inactivity which has been permitted to exist in this direction since the war broke out. I said last night that it was deplorable. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce objected to that. I repeat that it is deplorable that a Government representing 8,000,000 people, governing a country which has thousands of miles of coast line, administering the affairs of a people iwho, not so many years ago, turned out merchant vessels which were the pride of Canada and which sailed upon every sea, should remain idle and inactive so far as this important question is concerned, while they see month toy month and year by year the vessels flying the Canadian flag disappearing from the ocean. I appeal in the utmost seriousness to the Government, even at this late date, to take some effective steps towards encouraging the building of Ships in Canada and towards restoring, in
)

some measure at all events, our mercantile marine to its former position. 1 may be blamed tor bringing up this matter too often; but it is of such vast and vital importance from a national standpoint that no member of the House is doing his duty if he fails to .bring it to the attention of Parliament so long as nothing is being done. The ears of the ministers cannot be so deaf that if one beeps talking to them and pressing this upon their attention, they will mot at last pay 'heed to what the representatives of the people in this Parliament may say to them upon this important subject. . .	*
It was stated by .my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he was waiting for suggestions. That is not *creditable to the Government. Do not let them be so doubtful as to which is the best course to pursue that they will do nothing. Let them get to work. Whatever reasonable proposition they may submit to the House for the establishment of a Canadian mercantile marine will, I am sure, be cheerfully supported by hon. members on both sides. Only let them get to work; let them do something; let them show that they appreciate the situation which exists to-day .and the deplorable condition which will exist to a greater extent not many months from now if this war continues.
There are many ways in which shipbuilding may be encouraged. One most important way is by placing all materials which enter into the building of ships upon the free list, so that' we may relieve as far as possible the burdens upon those who are willing to engage in that work. I have it on reliable authority that if the Government will take off the duty on machinery, engines and boilers of the most modern type, which are necessary for shipbuilding, there are men in Canada ready to go to work without delay. Of course, the building of steel vessels would take longer than the building of wooden vessels; but the Canadian people, who, as we know, have the instinct of shipbuilding, would be able within a very few months to build wooden vessels; and, if the Government would allow the machinery for auxiliary power, the modern engine, to be brought in free of duty, I am satisfied that men would be found willing to engage in the building of wooden ships. Those ships would not, of course, last as long as steel vessels; but, if the war continues, they would pay for themselves, even at half the present rates, two or three times oyer in the course of a few years. My hon. friend knows that I pre-[Mr. Pugsley.J
sent that only as one way in which shipbuilding can 'be encouraged.
The Government might also, under the circumstances, having in view the national necessity of having more ships in the Canadian trade, encourage shipbuilding by the giving of bonuses. This session we are granting to the Government the enormous sum of $250,000,000, not entirely for war purposes, because they have asked us to give them authority to utilize a part of that amount for purposes which are not immediately connected with the war. One of the objects for which this money may be user: is:
Promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or otherwise.
It will be interesting to the House to be informed whether or not it is intended to apply any part of that amount either directly towards the building of ships or to the encouragement of shipbuilding. Certainly it would be quite possible for the Government, in the interest of Canada and for the purpose of encouraging the transportation of the food products of Canada to the Mother Country, to use a portion of that very large appropriation for that purpose.
I have seen it stated that if the war continues the question of the food supply of the Mother Country may become a serious one. Has the Government given any thought to that question? Only the other day a leading member of Parliament made the statement, which was surprising to me, and it may be surprising to other hon. members of this House, that at least one-half of the food supply of Great Britain to-day is carried on vessels belonging to neutral countries, and he expressed the' fear, which he said was becoming widespread, that as the activities of the German submarines increased and a larger proportion of vessels were destroyed, neutrals might hesitate to send their vessels to Great Britain, because they could employ them in other trade with almost equal profit, and with very much less danger than they would, necessarily encounter in their present trade. If this is a condition of affairs which is likely to exist in the future, how desirable it is that Canada should build up as quickly as possible a mercantile marine of her own ! Canada is in a position to supply the Mother Country with a large proportion of the foodstuffs she requires, as well as munitions of war, a!nd other supplies and manufactures which

may be required. Canada is vitally interested, not only from the standpoint of the Empire, but from the standpoint of the producers of our own country, in having ail reasonable facilities for the transportation of our products to the Mother Country and the Allies. This matter, therefore, presents itself not only from the standpoint of encouraging Canadian shipbuilding, thus giving employment to Canadian shipwrights, not only from the- standpoint of the Canadian producer, to whom it is desirable to afford the opportunity of sending his products to the Mother Country at as cheap a rate and in as large quantities as possible, but it is also important from the standpoint of the Empire, because an adequate food supply for the Mother Country and cur Allies is of vital importance in connection with the conduct of the war.
I desire to submit these views again to the Government, because this seemed to be a proper time, when the Estimates of the Naval Service Department were under consideration. I wish to congratulate my hon. friend and the Government that, notwithstanding the election assurances they gave prior to the election of 1911, that if the Conservative-Nationalist party should come into power they would at once take the necessary steps to repeal the Naval Service Act of 1910, they have not thought it in the interests of the countiy to repeal that Act. M,y hon. friend from Kings, P.E.I., (Mr. J. J. Hughes) reminds me that although that assurance was given in the House, yet there are times when the necessities of the country, and the necessities of the great Empire of which Canada forms so important a part, would justify members in breaking their word who ordinarily would like to see their pledges carried out. Hon gentlemen opposite could well say to the people of this country and to themselves that they were justified in taking that course in the interests of the country which they are serving, and for whose interests they ought to have the highest regard. I congratulate the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Government that these pledges were not carried out, and that the Naval Act stands on the statute-book to-day, and that this Government, without asking for further legislation, is in a position to encourage the building of war vessels, submarines, cruisers, torpedo-boat destroyers, patrol boats, or whatever else might be required. This Government, by reason of their not being so blind to the interests of the country as to repeal the
Naval Service Act, are in a position to go ahead to-day with what is in the best interests of their country in this respect. Without unduly finding fault, it is necessary in this eonnection to express one's regret that since the war broke out they have allowed twenty months to pass without taking one step in this direction; they have neglected to take any step in this direction ever since they came into office in October, 1911. Let me ask them now, before it is too late, to devise and submit to Parliament some plan which will enable them to undo, even in some small measure, the wrong which during these years they have committed against Canada. Let me urge them to take steps at once to provide in some measure, however inadequate, for the defence of the coasts of Canada and of our trade, and for the building up of a Canadian mercantile marine, which I am sure would prove of inestimable advantage to Canada and of the greatest possible service to the Empire.
I think the minister said in his statement that .the department had bought some 19 motor-boats.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not bought, but chartered.
Were these boats Canadian-built?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Chartered for the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, they are chartered
from time to time as they are needed.
Have any steamboats been bought by the department outside of Canada since the war began?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We did not buy them outside of Canada, but they came from outside of Canada.
They had been brought in before the Government bought them?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not very long before.

Apparently they were
brought in by some party who resold them to the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is not it. I shall be very glad to give my hon. friend all the facts privately, but for reasons, the sufficiency of which my hon. friend would recognize, this is a matter that cannot be put on Hansard or in the newspapers.

I do not wish the minister to say anything that it would not be

dn the interest of tiie country to divulge. Did the parties who brought these boats into Canada have to pay duty on them?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: You can generally trust the Customs Department to look after the collection of duties.

Except at Morrisburg.
Mr.'TURRIFF: If these were motorboats-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They were not motor-boats.
If they had been motorboats they might have been brought in on those scow-loads of goods that entered Canada without the knowledge of the Customs Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They could not do that.

The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) suggests that by way of encouraging shipbuilding in this country the Government might, under the present war conditions, remove the duty on machinery and on everything that would enter into the building of wooden or iron ships in Canada. The matter has been discussed during this session, but so far we have not been able to get any statement from the Government as to their policy in this regard. I would go a little further than the hon. member for St. John, and suggest that vessels built in other countries, in the British Isles, for instance, should be allowed to come in absolutely free of duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Vessels built in the old
country come into Canada free of duty. No duty is imposed on the vessel or any portion of it. The contents, even to the dishes and napkins and things of that kind, come in duty free.

Not from the United
States?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, from Great Britain.
I am glad to hear that. Do I understand that all materials entering into the building of vessels in Canada come in free of duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. The plates, shapes,
and things of that kind would come dn free of duty, but the machinery would not.
The Government are reversing their ordinary attitude on this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That has been the law for very many years.

I have heard my hon.
friends spend hours arguing that all this work should be done in Canada, yet here is a case where they actually discriminate against the building of ships in this country. Since the Government allows vessels built in Britain to come in free of duty, why should they not allow the material that would enter into the construction of vessels in Canada to come in free of duty? This would be doing something to start an industry in Canada the result of which would be increased business, increased manufacturing, increased labour for our men. What I particularly wish to point out is the extent to which this matter affects the people of Canada, more especially the people from the part of the country that I represent. We are to-day paying over 40 cents a bushel for the carrying of our wheat to the old country. According to reports in the newspapers, two or three British vessels are sent to the bottom every day by German submarines. If this keeps on for another year, where are we going to be? How are we going to get our produce .over to the Old Country? That is a matter that Britain is interested in just as much as we are, and no doubt Britain is 5 p.m. doing everything in her power to keep up the construction of merchant vessels in order to meet this wastage. The destruction of British and neutral vessels by German submarines is much greater to-day than it was six months ago or three months ago, much greater than it has been at any period during the war. Tramp steamers capable of carrying from 4,000 to 8,000 tons could very easily be built in Canada; in some parts of the country vessels of that size and of larger sizes are built. Vessels of this kind are quite capable of navigating the Atlantic, and there is no question that they could be built and completely equipped in Canada. The Government should encourage the building of ships in Canada in the interest of the cities where the ship-yards would be established, in the interest of the Empire, and particularly in the interest of that portion of the Empire which is producing foodstuffs, that are just as necessary to the British Government in the matter of bringing the war to a successful issue as are guns and ammunition. We are absolutely unfair to our own people when we refuse to allow the material for the construction of vessels to come into Canada duty free, and we are not doing our duty to ourselves and the Empire when we

take no steps to encourage shipbuilding at a time like this. It takes only a very short time to build such a vessel as I have described.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have a good deal to learn in the matter of building vessels. Only three or four years ago the right hon. leader of the Government said that it would take fifty years to build a war vessel in Canada, but it was proved within the last year or so. that submarines could be built in Montreal in a few .months-submarines that are equal, I imagine, to those built in any other part of the world and better by far than the submarines my hon. friend bought for use at Victoria and Vancouver, which will not to-day go out very far from land. Besides, foT these submarines my hon. friend paid almost two prices. Hon. gentlemen have had an example shown them by an American firm coming to Montreal and building submarines for the British Government-an American firm doing what we say we cannot do, and doing it in one of our own cities. Surely there is something wrong when that state of affairs exists. I am not so- much .interested in the building of war vessels, because that is. a matter that the British Government can take care of at home. I think it was at Great Britain's request that these submarines were built in America. The hon. member for St. John pointed out that the war is not by any means over. I was one of those who thought that the war would not last up to the present time, but, like other men in the country, I knew absolutely nothing about it. I think we are realizing that Kitchener was pro-bably nearer the truth than most men when he said that the war would last at least three years. It does not look today as if we were near the end of it. In my judgment the only way we shall bring it to an end will be by wearing Germany out financially; I do not think that we are going to. drive the Germans back and force the way to Berlin. If the Government are alive to their duties and responsibilities, they will, out of the $250,000,000 that we purpose voting in this House, or out of an additional vote if they want it, do something to encourage the. building of ships in Canada, either the smaller war vessels or commercial vessels-more particularly the latter-and so enable us to help ourselves, to help the Empire, and to help bring the war to a successful conclusion as quickly as possible.

I was pleased to hear within the last day or two that the Minister of Trade and Commerce intended to have discussed, the question of ocean tonnage and ocean rates. I heard, also, a portion of the speech of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), and that of the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Turriff). I agree that every shipyard in Canada ought to be engaged in building ships that would help to relieve the pressure in regard to ocean tonnage and ocean freight. It is surprising what we can do in Canada in the way of shipbuilding if we do not attempt it on too large a scale. For instance, we have built steamships in the inland ports of Ontario that can be taken apart aind so taken through the canals, put together in Montreal, and that make first class freighters on the Atlantic. A Canadian company has routed a number of boats intended for inland navigation, on the Atlantic, and they are helping to relieve the pressure, and some of them have been taken into the service of the Admiralty for war purposes. If we can build those ships in our inland shipyards we ought to be building them now, because the pressure is increasing, and at the rate at which ships are being destroyed now there wili be a greater necessity hereafter and we shall need more ships, to take-our produce across the Atlantic. I did not hear all of the speech of the hon. gentleman in reference to the discussion in this House some years ago when the proposal to furnish dreadnoughts was up, but at that time I thought the opportunity had arrived, by reason of the policy introduced by the Government, of creating a great shipbuilding industry in Canada. I believe that we can build ships in this country. We are building them, and we can build a great many more. To my mind national policy certainly calls for the development of shipbuilding in Canada. Whatever legislation or policy would bring that about would certainly meet with the approval of the country, and I hope, the Government have some policy in that matter. Probably when the Minister of Trade and Commerce comes to discuss this subject he may have some suggestion to make.
I desire to bring to the attention of the Minister of the Naval Service and of this House tiie part that Canada can play in the building of airships. In Toronto today there are being built the finest and best aeroplanes used in the service of

Great Britain in the war in Europe. I have been at the factory there, and have seen proba'bly 600 men engaged in building airships. They are built on the most modern specifications, and they are so successful, the plans are so well drawn-I believe the British Admiralty had a hand in the drawing of the plans-that it is not necessary to experiment with them; they are so accurately built and have succeeded so well that they are shipped from Toronto just as they are completed, now at the rate of three a week, and I hope that within a short time at least six a week will be sent. Whoever is responsible for that work being done should receive credit for it. I hope that the Government are entitled to some of that credit. I know that an association of gentlemen in Toronto have taken up this question of aviation and the part that Canada could play in building airships. There is this advantage about the industry, that in going into it we start even with all other nations. It is a new industry. We have the draftsmen, the mechanics, the factories and every facility for the building of airships. The aeroplanes that are now going forward from Toronto weigh 4,000 pounds. They will carry three men and 2,000 pounds of war material. They are, next to the dirigibles, probably the most efficient flying machines being made to-day. We can build these aeroplanes; we have proved it; and I hope the Government will take up this question of building them. It is weil know that the use of cavalry in war for scouting purposes has been largely discontinued. The place of cavalry on land and of the scouting vessel at sea is taken by these aeroplanes; and, that being the case, and we being able to build them, I hope that the minister will devise a pelicy-if the war is to continue, and we know that the end is not in sight-which will stimulate still further the production of aeroplanes in Canada. They could be built in Toronto, in Montreal, in St. John, and in Halifax. The gentlemen who are connected with this industry in Toronto are very anxious to see a school of aviation organized in Canada in connection with the naval college at Halifax. I hope the Minister of Marine will take up that suggestion, which has been made by this association in Toronto, and that we shall have a school in Halifax devoted to aviation, because we are able to turn out pilots for these vessels equal to those turned out in the old country; and some of the Canadians who have gone to the front as pilots of airships have showp themselves to be just as competent 
in the airship as our troops are in the field. I trust that before this session is over the minister and the Government will be able to say that they have considered this question of aviation and the building of airships, and that they will do something that will still further stimulate this industry. Only two or three days ago I heard that the company now building airships in Toronto have received another order from the British Government and that still other orders will be forthcoming. But while I am glad to see that the industry is developing in Canada, I fear that our Government has not sufficiently encouraged this branch of war production. The British Government is encouraging it, and giving orders for aeroplanes in this country. 1 think that this Government, if they wish Canada to play the part in the war which it is competent in every way to do, should encourage a school of aviation and the building of these flying machines in Toronto. If they do that they will make a substantial contribution to the strength of the Empire and materially improve the part we ourselves will be able to play in this struggle. So I trust that both the question of shipbuilding in Canada, in v hick I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce is very much interested, and the question of aviation, will receive the attention of the Government; and that some kind of advanced national policy in respect to both of these things will be announced at an early date.
Mr. HAZEN While I have no objection to a discussion of the question of the construction of ships for commercial purposes, it is not a matter that' properly arises on the items of the Naval Service. It is a matter that more properly fails within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I understand that, either yesterday or the day before, an understanding was reached in the House, as a number of members wished to discuss this subject while my hon. friend's Estimate,' were under consideration, that one Estimate should stand until Monday or Tuesday, when it was understood there would be a general discussion of the subject of the construction in Canada of ships for commercial purposes.
1 may say, in answer to some statements that have been made, that there is no doubt whatever that, if the war continued, and freights remained at the present figure, it would be only a short time-freights having increased so much since the outbreak of the war-before ships of that charactep, if con-

structed and placed in commission, would practically pay for themselves. But it is not so easy, and not possible within so short a time as my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) suggested, to have a commercial ship constructed and put in commission. I am referring to ships of 7,000 tons and 10,000 tons, which iny hon. friend mentioned. I am in a position to tell him that if he entered into a contract with a Canadian shipbuilding company tomorrow to build ships of that character, he would find, in the first place, the prices exceedingly high because of the very high cost of steel, and it would not be until well after the opening of navigation on the St. Lawrence in 1917 that the ships would be ready to be placed in commission and to do the work for which they Were intended. I mention that, not as an insuperable objection, but for the information of my hon. friend, which may be useful in the discussion when it comes on next week In the meantime, if the war should come to an end before commercial ships could be constructed, it would be reasonable to expect a falling-off in the high freight rates that are being paid at/the present time, though my own belief is that, in view of the destruction of commercial ships since the outbreak of war, freights would remain above the normal figure for some time to come.
My hon. friend from Assiniboia alluded to the submarines that were purchased ' and that are now at Victoria, and he suggested that they could not go to sea. I want to remove that idea from the mind of my hon. friend, and to tell him that we have daily reports in the department of what these submarines are doing, showing that they are most efficient vessels, and able to do what other submarines are able to do anywhere, and take equally long voyages. The price paid for the two submarines was $1,150,000. Perhaps my hon. friend from Assiniboia heard my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) say that twenty submarines, the contract for which was given by the British Government to the Fore River Shipbuilding Company, or to Mr. Schwab, and which were partly built at the Fore River shipyard, partly by the Union Shipbuilding Company at San Francisco, and assembled at Montreal, cost $10,000,000. That would -be $500,000 each. They were submarines of practically the same size as those acquired by the Canadian Government at Seattle, and yet the contract price was $10,000,000. I think my
hon. friend will find that if the price the British Government paid the Canadian Vickers Company for the use of their shipyard was added, it would have added considerably to the contract price that was paid to Mf. iStohwab. I point that out to my hon. friend, as I know that he has no desire to make statements that are not in accordance with the facts, and he was probably .misled-
Will the minister state the length of the submarines which were built at Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They were practically of
the same length. They were submarines of a class similar to those we purchased, and, as I have said, a portion of them came from the Fore River shipyard, and a portion from the Union Company's shipyard at San Francisco. In fact, the gentleman who was in charge of the assembling of the submarines at Montreal was Vice-president and General Manager of the Union Shipbuilding Company of San Francisco. But when he considers that the British Government purchased twenty submarines, that they were not purchased in a hurry, that they cost on an average the same as the submarines purchased by the Canadian Government' at Seattle, and that they were practically of the same type and size, I think my hon. friend from Assiniboia will come to the conclusion that although the two submarines purchased at Seattle were bought in a hurry, and there was no time to dicker about the /price, and that the matter of price was not of very much importance in the circumstances, the Government of Canada made a pretty fair bargain.

I am not relying upon
anything that I heard in this House; I am relying absolutely on the statement made by the expert of the Chilian Government, as to the price that the Chilian Government was to pay for the submarines if they were up to standard, that he had inspected the submarines and found that they were not up to specifications, that therefore they were refused by the Chilian Government, although they had been almost paid for, and that the price to the Chilian Government was very much below what this Government paid for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That statement is disputed; but, apart from that, I refer my hon. friend to the evidence which was given before Sir Charles Davidson, which was referred to in this House on a former occasion, by



men who aie experts in Tegard to submarines, all of whom testified to the effect that these two submarines were well fitted for the service for which they were intended, and as efficient as any submarines of the class to be obtained anywhere. The fact is, that these submarines have done excellent work, and I do not know what purpose is to be served, from a party standpoint, or from any other standpoint, by decrying them, and endeavouring to make it appear that they are not equal to the work for which they were intended.
Hon. gentlemen opposite did not take that view when they talked about the tinpot navy.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: and 'Commerce allowed the $1,000,000 item to stand over for the purpose of possibly being able to announce that he had entered into a contract for the proposed service. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that there would be an opportunity of discussing the question of shipbuilding later on, but I do not know that it would be more appropriate in connection with those estimates than with the estimates of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the commercial side of it.
Except that simply it refers to the subsidy for the service.

I appreciate
very much the statement made by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in regard to aviation; but I wish to point out in reply that it is more a matter of the army than of the navy, and that as such it was brought before the Department of Militia and Defence, but has not received very much encouragement in that direction. The whole evidence of this war emphasizes the importance of flying in warfare. I have been in touch with gentlemen connected with the Admiralty who are engaged in the construction of airships, and their testimony is that we in Canada can establish just as good a flying school and build just as useful flying machines as in any other country. While he says that a flying machine is not of very much account in relation to navigation, I wish to point out that if the German navy broke away from its refuge in the Kiel canal and passed the British line and got into the Atlantic, it would raid our Canadian ports, and especially cities such as Halifax and St. John, and would be able to do great damage in'that direction. The only way, not of heading off such an invasion, but of giving intimation of it, would be by a corps of flying machines manned by Canadians and men trained in Panada. So that the matter of defence in the way of flying machines comes right home to us. The manufacture of flying machines is something we can do as well as any other country, and we start on an equal footing with every otheii country in regard to this matter. Therefore, to my mind, it is worthy of encouragement. With the exception of the engines, those machines which are turned out in Toronto are all made in Canada. The engines can soon be made here, and in 
that way we shall be able to turn out probably the most active, certainly the most useful, of the new arms of warfare that are being developed in this war, and I trust that the minister will reconsider the question and talk it over with his colleagues and see if it be not possible to start a school of aviation in connection with the naval college at Halifax.
What number of men did the miriister state had been recruited for the naval service of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend mean the Imperial service?
Well, I think it was both.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The figures I gave were the number who had been recruited for the Imperial service, and I think they were something, like 600.
And for the Canadian service since the war broke out?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think about 1,000.
What has become of those who have been recruited for the Canadian service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are employed on the different ships throughout the country- upon the Rainbow, upon the submarines, upon the Shearwater, upon our patrol service on the Atlantic and on the Pacific, upon our mine-sweeping service, upon our examination service, and upon the different other services that we are carrying on.

speechtext:
The men who enlist are
purely volunteers. At the opening of the

war, when we wanted recruits, we let that fact be known in Toronto. There was a gentleman there who volunteered his services, and most efficient services they were. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

Bill No. 24, respecting the Toronto, Niagara and Western Railway Company-Mr. Morphy-in committee.
On section 1-short title:

We have heard a good deal in committee and in the House about the competition that these roads would exercise as against a project of the province of Ontario. It is my view that where additional transportation facilities are to be afforded they should be given in the newer parts of Canada, where railroad facilities are badly needed, rather than in those parts of Ontario and the eastern provinces where adequate transportation facilities are already provided. The Canadian Northern Railway, the promoters of which are back of the Bills which are before the committee, was intended primarily as a colonisation road to serve Western Canada. In my constituency they have charters for roads which have not been built, although people [DOT]have been attracted to those districts in anticipation of railway facilities being provided. Many of the people are still miles away from transportation facilities, waiting for the Canadian Northern Railway Company to construct lines in that section of the country. It is my view that they should build lines to serve those districts before they attempt to compete in districts in the province of Ontario which are already fairly well supplied with transportation facilities. I hope

that under the amendment to the Railway Act these roads will not be given the opportunity to spend money in constructing competitive lines in districts like the Niagara peninsula, and that their efforts will be concentrated in providing roads in those districts where transportation facilities are absolutely needed. Many complaints are heard about the need of transportation facilities in Western Canada. During the last year there was an extremely heavy crop, and in the country north of Medicine Hat, where a charter has been granted for the construction of a Canadian Northern line, the farmers had to draw their grain 70 or 80 miles to the nearest station. Although the charter for this Canadian Northern line has been granted, and although the bonds have been guaranteed by the provincial Government, nothing is being done. There is another section of country south of Medicine Hat where a Canadian Northern line has been projected, and nothing is being done. Yet the Canadian Northern Railway Company ask this Parliament for the privilege of constructing a railroad in a -district which is already well supplied with transportation facilities. I am not opposing the Bill, but I want to place my views on record in this regard. I am not in sympathy with the Mackenzie and Mann interests attempting to construct a line in a province already supplied with railroads, especially in competition with the HydroElectric project of the province of Ontario. I do not think that we should interfere with the desires of the people of the province of Ontario in that respect. Their legislature has unanimously declared that they want these bills defeated, that they want to have an opportunity of constructing radial lines in that province. In my opinion, they should be allowed to do that, and these particular interests should devote their attention to the needs of districts that are not already supplied with transportation facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
There is no difference of
opinion between the hon. member and myself as to the necessity for supplying the different parts of the country with railways. I agree absolutely that there should be no duplicating of railways, and, in addition, that running rights should be granted over an existing railway to a new railway in order to avoid the unnecessary expense of constructing a new line. The Canadian Northern railway is a system composed

of about 10,000 miles of railway, probably 7,000 of that being in Western Canada. The hon. member was not in the House when certain legislation went through; but let me say to him, as a member in this House at the time that legislation was passed, that I think the mistake that was made was this. The Canadian Northern railway was organized in Western Canada, being entirely a Western Canada scheme. The company built branch lines of railway throughout Western Canada, and their eastern terminus was to be Fort William and Port Arthur.' That was the point they expected to reach, and they built their road to that point. Then the Grand Trunk Railway Company realized the great opportunities for railway development in the great Northwest and wished to enter that field. Legislation was introduced in this House providing for a railway, under the control of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, from North Bay to Winnipeg and through to Prince Rupert. There is no doubt that the Canadian Northern Railway Company did its best to arrange with the Government of the day that one line of railway should be built from North Bay to Fort William or to Winnipeg, and then that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should take over the Canadian Northern system and operate its western branches, instead of building a line from North Bay to Winnipeg and through to the West, closely parallelling the Canadian Northern railway and the Canadian Pacific railway. The Canadian Northern Railway Company urged on the Government that if the Grand Trunk would take over their system in the West, a great and unnecessary expenditure of money would be avoided. Another suggestion was that one railway should be built from North Bay to Winnipeg for the common use of all lines. That arrangement, of course, was not made, with the result that an agreement was made under which the Grand Trunk Pacific railway was built from Moncton through to Prince Rupert. What was the result of that? The Canadian Northern railway had a very extensive system of branch lines throughout the West. I must admit that those lines were not as well built as the Grand Trunk .Pacific and the Canadian Pacific railway, many of them being colonization roads, but^yet they were of great advantage to that country and carried out an immense quantity of grain to Fort William and Port Arthur. But when the Canadian

Northern railway got the grain to Port Arthur, what were they to do with it? During the summer season they could get it out 'by boat, but in winter their whole system from Fort William through the West was tied up from the 1st of December until the 1st of May, or the opening of navigation. If they wished to send out their grain by rail during the winter season, they were at the -mercy of the other two railways. That is the position they took with the late Government, and our predecessors then gave the Canadian Northern Railway a charter to build from Fort William and Port Arthur to the East, instead of insisting on their acquiring running rights over the Canadian Pacific railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific from Port Arthur to the East. They gave them a charter and advanced, I think, $30,000,000 in order to start the construction of their railway from Port Arthur to Ottawa. When the present Government came into power, we found that the money 'had been arranged for and the railway commenced, so that its construction could not be stopped.
The Canadian Northern Railway Company were in a similar position in reference to a western outlet to the Pacific ocean. The Government authorized and assisted in the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific through to the Pacific coast, and the -Canadian Northern system was at the mercy of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific Railway in respect to through western traffic, just as it was in respect to shipments from Fort William and Port Arthur to the East. When this Government came into power, we found the Canadian Northern system with a railway not built but under way. Enormous amounts of money had been granted by the Government, and we had no alternative but to see that system completed. When the Canadian Northern got down to Toronto with freight from Vancouver, say through freight from the Orient, they had no means of getting that through freight, which might be Touted to New York or the West Indies, from 'Toronto t-o Buffalo to hand it over to the American roads. They have no American connection to-day, and therefore they are trying to make this short connection between Toronto and Buffalo in order to have a complete system.
-Surely these Bills are not for the purpose of allowing this road to go into the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Certainly. These Bills are to allow a connection between Canada and the United States, such as all transcontinental railways have. Surely the hon. member for Edmonton does not mean to say that a railway like the Canadian Pacific railway, running from Vancouver to St. John, or a railway like the Grand Trunk Pacific, running from Prince Rupert to Halifax, should not be allowed to have any connection with American roads wherever there is interchangeable freight? Surely the hon. member must admit that a road carrying freight sent from the Orient through our own Canadian territory should have some way of getting out to New York if the cargo is consigned to New York. That is what I mean by having an American connection. They have none now.
' Mr. OLIVER: I thought it was the fixed policy of this Government not to permit Canadian freight to be diverted to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The hon. member knows that this is not diverted. I stated that the freight was consigned to New.York; that is why this connection was asked for. The only difference of opinion is that some say that this portion of the railway, fifty or sixty miles in extent, could be built by the Hydro-Electric and operated by them. I was one of those who differed from that view. The Hydro-Electric could operate radial lines, but this railway will have a lot of freight traffic. Radial lines are more for rural districts and city districts. To carry this class of freight it would be necessary to have long, heavy trains, with fifty or sixty cars. I think there should be a regular steam system. At present, between Toronto and Niagara Falls, the Canadian Pacific railway and Grand Trunk trains run over the Grand Trunk line be- ' tween Toronto and Hamilton, which is double tracked. From the information I have I think that these two railways, certainly the Grand' Trunk, are taxed to its fullest capacity at the present time. Between Hamilton and Niagara Falls there is the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo railway and the Grand Trunk, and the Canadian Pacific railway trains and those of another company run over that road. I believie there is room for another line between Toronto and Niagara Falls, and I feel satisfied that now that the matter is in the hands of the' Railway Commission, these Bills, or any other Bills that come before it in the future, will receive fair considera-

tion. If any objection is raised to the findings of the Kailway Commission there is an appeal to the Governor in Council. I would like to see this Bill go through, so that the Railway Commission can give the new line a fair trial. If it works well we will have no more trouble in the future, so far as the parallelling of railways is concerned. If it does not work satisfactorily then we can change or rescind the law.
Has the minister made any effort to induce this company to bring their railway to a Canadian port instead of diverting to Buffalo on the way to New York?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend knows the situation just as well as I do. In the legislation which we put through this House while he was a member, there is a clause which provides that they must bring their freight to Montreal and Quebec in the summer, and there is an understanding that it be handed over to the Intercolonial for St. John and Halifax. It is also in the knowledge of my hon. friend that they had a line of freight steamers, some eight, ten or a dozen, and two' fine passenger steamers, running to St. John and Halifax for some years. Then there was the Uranian line. Every member knows that so far as the railway is concerned they have no American port; their ports being entirely Canadian-Montreal and Quebec in the Summer, and .St. John and Halifax in the winter. But as I stated before, this refers only to freight destined for American points, Chicago, New York, or other cities. In the case of a large railway system, such as this is, there is no doubt a large amount of inter-changeable American freight going from the main lines or branch limes to the United States, and vice versa, from' the United States to Canada. The loss of that freight w'ould, of course, be a great disadvantage to this railway.

The point I desired to make was that these railway companies should toe made, first of all, to supply the route where facilities are most needed. It is necessary in the interests of our country that these facilities should toe provided in new districts into which, people have moved, and where railways are needed to develop the country. If the people of Ontario are prepared to provide such facilities in their province, they should be allowed to' do so, but they should also allow this company to provide facilities in another 
part of the country where they are urgently needed. I did not know that the Minister of Railways was a pessimist, but he seems to be pessimistic about the railway situation in this country. It may be a gloomy situation at the present moment, when financial conditions are toad, and there is very little development going on; but
1	am an optimist, and I believe that the railways which have been constructed in this country will justify expectations as soon as immigrants begin to come as they came in the past. Why, the crop of last ye.ar could not be handled by the existing railroads; it will not toe entirely removed from the western country until the coming harvest. We have millions upon millions of acres of land in the West still to toe settled and cultivated, and when that land is .settled and cultivated railways will be absolutely needed, and they will earn profits. At the time the Canadian Pacific railway was constructed, there were criticism and doubt as to its possibilities, but history has shown that the building of that railway was warranted, and I am certain that history will show that the construction of the other railways was warranted, if we handle the situation properly. We have no adequate conception of the possibilities and prospects of western Canada. If we have a crop like that of last year for the next five or six years, the natural resources of this country will be enriched to an extent that we cannot at present estimate. The prospects of this year's crop are that while we may not have such a tremendous acreage as we had last year, there will be a great crop, and the railroads will be kept busy until 1917 or 1918 getting it out.
Was the Rocky Mountain section of the Canadian Northern railway started when the present Government came into office	'

On the preamble:

Before the preamble is adopted, I wish to say that there was a great deal of opposition in Ontario to these two Bills, especially on behalf of the Hydro-Electric Commission and the Hydro-Radial system of railways now-under construction in that province. That commission, having identified with it the municipalities and the Government of Ontario, through Sir Adam Beck and others, protested against the incorporation of these companies. Apparently a compromise has been arranged, under which the Canadian Northern Railway Company will still be able to reach the Niagara river. But the result of the opposition which was shown here by Sir Adam Beck and his friends has been effective, perhaps not to the full extent; but what Sir Adam Beck desired has been accomplished and the working out of the provisions of these two Bills is now to be in the hands of the Railway Commission, which will be tested with powder to say whether the roads are needed, to say whether joint user of existing lines will not be sufficient, and in other ways to protect the rights of the municipalities and of the Hydro-Electric Commission.
I wish just to say that in the Legislature of Ontario yesterday the Government announced that they had closed forever the use of water-powers by private corporations now- having rights to develop power, and that all the power in Ontario hereafter is to be consecrated to public use. Furthermore, it was announced that the plan of Sir Adam Beck for the development of the greatest system of water-pow'er in America was to be conducted by the people of the province, and that these powers were to be devoted to the use of the municipalities and the railways of the province. We hope that the result of the development of the wateT-powers in Ontario, especially of the Niagara river, by the Hydro-Electric Commission as a public proposition will be sufficient not only to rim all the factories, and to light all the hohses and towns in Ontario, but also to drive most of the railways of that province. This is great and progressive legislation. I have no doubt that public ownership of railways is coming in this country, and that we in the province of Ontario will be able not only to develop a system of local railways but to supply power at the cheapest possible rate for the handling of all the traffic of Ontario. There was a time not many years ago when men who advocated that were said to be visionaries. Yet it is' being
worked, to-day in Ontario, it is a success there, it has been so successful as applied to power and light that we now know that it will be successful as applied to railway traffic, and we hope and expect that it will not only be successful to the extent that we will be able, by a public-owned proposition, to develop and supply enough power to run railways in southern Ontario, but that eventually all these railways will be owned and controlled by the people of that province.

I notice there are two Bills on the Order Paper following each other, one relating to the Salvation Army in Canada East, and the other relating to the Salvation Army in Canada West. If the mover would explain the situation in a few words as to both it would be an advantage.

These Bills were introduced in the Senate and were passed in their original form. When they came to the committee of the House of Commons some objection was taken because they did not divide the country, making one jurisdiction for Eastern Canada and the other for Western Canada. The objection seemed, to be well taken, and after careful consideration on the part of the .committee and some concessions on the part of those representing the Salvation Army, the objections were met and are embodied in the Bill. The whole matter in connection with both Bills is simply one of internal government resulting from the rapidly-developing work of the Salvation Army in Eastern and Western Canada. The Salvation Army obtained an Act of incorporation some years ago, but owing to the rapid increase in the work of the society they found it almost impossible to - govern so large a corporation without a division. The Bill gives them a western board of management

and an eastern 'board of management. In the two Bills, one of which is now before the committee, that is being embodied. It is not any public concern. There is no variation from the rights of the Salvation Army and no increase of powers from those granted in the incorporation of the Army in Canada some years ago.

If the minister would permit me to ask a question relating to the previous item, would he be good enough to give the House the benefit of his conclusions, based on the surveys that have been made, as to the navigability of Hudson bay and the straits, and the season during which navigation is practicable?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Since 1910 the Department
of the Naval Service has published in each annual report the results of observations in Hudson bay made by the officers of the survey steamer in these waters, and has also published extracts from " logs " on different vessels navigating in Hudson bay, These reports give a large amount of information as to ice conditions in the bay and in the straits, -and as to the dates of opening and closing of navigation. Any one interested in the conditions of navigation in these waters would do well to study these reports attentively.
Any conclusions as to average conditions must be based on observations extending over long series of years. The object of these Teports has been to gather together the available information, and place it before the public. Information of a similar nature, though perhaps not quite so accurate, was given by the observers attached to Commander Gordon's Expedition in 1884-86.
Some newspapers this year piade great capital out of -a few sentences contained in the last reports submitted by Mr. Anderson, but it would have been better to follow the annual reports made since 1910, so as to obtain ia better idea of average conditions which existed in different parts of the straits and of the bay, and so be able to gain a better appreciation of the conditions which exist in these waters. -
While conditions vary considerably from year to year, the following information may be of interest. Commander Gordon, as -a result of three voyages to Hudson straits in 1884-5-6, considered that for specially built vessels, fortified to meet the ice conditions, the season of navigation would be about three months, beginning in the first week

of July .and closing in the first week of October. In 1910 the C.G.S. ice breaker Stanley passed through Hudson strait between the 18th and 31st July, and encountered 200 miles of heavy drift ice from Cape Prince of Wales to Digges Island; and the same extent of heavy drift ice was encountered in Hudson bay. On the return trip, about the 30th July, a few hours after leaving Port Nelson, the heaviest ice yet encountered was entered and proved to be about 90 miles across. No exact information is available as to the close of navigation in that year, but the officer at Eric Cove estimated that a vessel might have passed through the straits on the 15th November.
In 1911 the first ship, the sealer Beothic, passed through Hudson strait between the 25th and 29th July, meeting extensive fields of winter and Arctic ice southeast from Big island. The passage after this was fairly open, but ice fields were noticed to the south in Hudson bay. The Acadia crossed Hudson bay, homeward, about the end of September without noticing any field ice and cleared Cape Cliidley on October'10th with no ice in sight.
In 1912 the first ship, the sealer Beothic, passed through Hudson straits between the 15th and 20th July and met considerable drift ice. The last ship passed out between the 2nd and 6th November, with no ice in sight. Ships navigating this region during the latter part of July reported that drift ice was encountered, in some eases extremely heavy and closely packed. On the 2nd August the Minto reported a field of ice a couple of miles across off cape Prince of Wales. Extensive ice fields were reported in Hudson bay to the south. Fox channel ice was reported at the west entrance of the strait on the 25th October.
In 1913 the first steamer, the sealer Bona-venture, entered Hudson strait on the 16th July, arriving at Port Nelson on the 6th August, having met with very heavy ice on the trip. Extensive ice fields were reported in Hudson strait on the 8th August by the sealer Naseopie and scattered ice fields by the sealer Bonaventure on the 16th August. The Naseopie reported extensive ice fields off Mansel and Digges islands on the 1st October, requiring considerable bunting to force a passage. On the 22nd October the Acadia found the passage at the west entrance to the straits practically closed by heavy ice, and, though specially strengthened, sustained considerable damage forcing a way through. The tramp steamer Alette met with ice north of Mansel island
on the 10th October, and stove in her bow. She returned to Port Nelson in a sinking condition and was finally beached.
In 1914 the first ship, the sealer Bonaventure, parsed through Hudson strait between the 1st and 8th August, and the last ship, the Bonaventure, passed out of the strait on the 22nd October.
From these extracts it might seem that specially constructed vessels can navigate the Hudson during probably three months of each year, the exact dates of opening and closing of navigation varying considerably.
As a result of the work accomplished by the Hydrographic Survey of late years, the charts of Hudson bay have been very considerably improved and special charts have been issued showing Port Churchill, Port Nelson and its approaches and various harbours which are available for refuge to Hudson straits.
It has been found that good water is available in Hudson straits and that its navigation presents no particular difficulties apart from the ice. The observations taken show that the magnetic compass is very unreliable in various parts of Hudson bay, and that captains of vessels must rely largely on observations to direct their ships in safety. By the aid of the published charts both Churchill and Nelson can be approached in safety and the Department of Marine has installed a number qf aids to navigation which have improved conditions in these waters very considerably. A wireless station is in operation at Port Nelson, which communicates with ships properly equipped and is of valuable assistance in that vicinity. It is proposed to erect other wireless stations in Hudson straits so as to afford continuous communication to vessels in these waters.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The reports show that the seasons vary. In some years there is a longer period of navigation than in others, and the dates of opening and closing of navigation vary. Summarizing the, whole thing, I think it is pretty clear from all these reports that there has not been a year when navigation was not reasonably practicable for a period of from two or three months. That is what the reports of observers who have been there, surveyors and others, would lead one to conclude.
That is about the time of navigation at Archangel, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At Archangel, I think, it is a little longer.

Did the minister take any advice from shipping people in regard to the practicability of navigation o.f Hudson, bay? I have heard a great many people who are accustomed to navigating the northern waters condemn the idea, and I should suppose that people having experience of that kind would be the best people for the minister to go to t-o find out what the chances of navigation in those waters are. There are many traders on the coasts of Canada who have for many years gone to the northern waters in the summer, and they must know more about the navigation there than people who- go up for a summer's trip, like the commanders of these steamers. Has the minister any scheme for establishing a fleet of ships to perform the service on the Hudson bay route after the railway' is completed, or does he expect to depend on private enterprise altogether for the providing of the ships? It will be of no use to have a railway to Hudson bay unless some one will provide ships to carry the cargoes to the market. If we are going to construct the road, it is of the greatest importance that we should look into, that question and see what is to happen when we have completed the road. We all want to make it a success, after putting our money into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I explained that the conclusion I came to is based on the reports of men who have been sent there to make examinations, and also on the logs of vessels that have gone in and out of Hudson bay. That is the best evidence that can be obtained. The hon. gentleman is right in saying that there are many people who think that from a commercial standpoint the project is not practicable. Time will tell whether that is the case or not. The members of this House, irrespective of party, evidently thought that the scheme was practicable, because both parties were pledged up to the hilt to build the Hudson Bay railway. Both parties agreed to it. I do not believe that any policy would appeal so strongly to men of the intelligence of the members of this House unless there was merit back of it. But there are, of course, people who are doubtful about all new enterprises, even in a country more or less known. It is well known.that it was predicted 50 or 60 years ago that railways
could not be successful in Canada because they could not be operated during the winter. That was said during the building of the Grand Trunk railway, by m'en of position and ordinary common sense in this country. The same thing has been said in respect of other progressive enterprises,. Something similar was said about the Canadian Pacific railway owing to the difficulties of construction in the mountain section, and I hope it will he found when this railway is built and the terminal facilities provided for grain, that a great deal o>f grain from the West will find its way to Europe by Hudson bay.
My bom. friend has referred to the need of steamers to carry the products away.
I concur in his statement, but I am hopeful that there will be people who, from a commercial standpoint, will find, it to their < interest, perhaps with some Government assistance, to put on vessels to carry wheat from Hudson bay; and I am sure that is a matter to which every attention will be paid by the Railway Department, which is to oper-ate the railway and will be responsible in that connection.

In the case of ail of these large enterprises to which the minister has alluded, engineers and men who made reports upon the project always estimated them at very much less than the final cost. It looks as if when men were sent out especially to make reports on such matters, they always looked upon the favourable side. 1 have had opportunity of speaking with some men who have acted as officers on the boats that went into Hudson bay, but whose duty was not to report, and the opinion I have heard expressed by them is that it is practically impossible to make a harbour at Port Nelson; that the sandbar there is neatly three miles in width, and that it shifts every summer, and may shift half a mile in 21 hours. Comparing it with Liverpool, where the sandbar is only a cable length in breadth, that would seem to present a very serious obstacle. At Liverpool they have three dredges at work night and day, one of them the most powerful in the world; and it is difficult for them to make navigation practicable.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Still, they have made a great harbour there by artificial 'means.

Because the trade there warrants it. If anything like the same trade could be developed a.t Port Nelson, perhaps such an expenditure would be war-

ranted there too; but if the statements I have heard are correct, and anything like the same proportion of dredging would be required, it would take a fleet of 50 or 60 dredges, working constantly, to keep the channel open. This information I have received from deep-sea captains who have had experience there, and if there is anything in their reports it is a serious condition of affairs.

I have understood that when the 'bon. 'member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) was Minister of Railways, he had a very careful examination made of the relative merits of Fort Churchill and Port Nelson, and the report of the engineer, Mr. Armstrong, I think it was, was very strongly in favour of Port Nelson as the terminus. I have always understood that while there is a sandbar there and difficulty about the channel, that is the port to which the sea captains gave preference. They did not go into Port Nelson, but anchored outside, and the chief engineer found another and a good channel which would be more easily navigated, and where comparatively little dredging work would require to be done. That is what I understood. We all know, too, that, after the present Minister of Railways took office, he visited Hudson bay, and inspected both Port Nelson and Fort Churchill with a view to exercising his own judgment upon the decision which the former
10 p.m. Minister of Railways had reached, and he came to the same conclusion as the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), that there would be no serious difficulty in approaching Port Nelson, and that a good harbour could be secured there.
Mr. HAZE'iN: Tire Hydrographic Survey ship went into Port Nelson and marked the channel with byoys, and I am told that other ships have now no trouble.

speechtext: Speaking of the navigation of the St. Lawrence river within the past thirty years, I was told that a man as well informed as the late Mr. Gladstone, speaking to a member of the Canadian Government in London when he was Colonial Secretary, expressed his regret that the dangers of navigation of the St. Lawrence was so great that that river could never become a successful route for commercial and passenger -ships. Mr, OLIVER:	Yes, the telegraph line

I hardly know which would be cheaper. In a district, with settlements at different points, a wire system would be better. You could have telegraph stations anywhere, whereas you could not have them with a wireless system. If it is a country that is growing, with communities springing up, a wire system would be better for ordinary commercial purposes. Of course,
the wireless telegraphic system which the Department of Marine administers is intended to aid navigation. We have stations along the Atlantic coast, up the- St. I.awrence, on the shores of the Great Lakes, and on the Pacific coast, extending from Victoria to the north, but they are all for the purpose of aiding navigation, and a very important aid they are. To my mind, wireless telegraphy is going to render safe the navigation of Hudson straits, and will be of greater advantage thpn lighthouses along that route, because the operatives will be able to convey information to the , ships going up and down as to the state of the ice and that sort of thing.
