speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is for the maintenance of the principal tidal stations in Eastern Canada and on the Pacific coast throughout the year, and the salaries of observers. Further tidal observations in the gulf of St. Lawrence and the bay of Fundy and also in British Columbia and on Hudson bay are made at tidal stations which are erected for the summer season. Tidal information is also obtained from other surveys, supplied with an outfit of instruments; thus also saving much expense to them. The results deduced from these observations improve the accuracy and scope of the tide tables which is a benefit to the commerce of the country. Observations are to be continued in the gut of Canso; and further observations of the currents in straits on the Pacific coast are to be obtained. Annual tide tables are prepared for Eastern Canada, for the Pacific coast and for Hudson bay. In addition to these complete tables, the following abridged editions are published in pocket size: Quebec and Father Point with data for the St. Lawrence; St. John, N.B., and the bay of Fundy; Vancouver and gulf of Georgia, With data for the narrows and passes of southern British Columbia. All these are widely distributed, amounting to 42,000 copies. In addition to the above, much information, especially on tide levels, is furnished to other departments, which saves them considerable expense, while only represented by extra work without expenditure in this survey. The information is published in the Tide Tables and in the Notices to Mariners which are issued from time.to time. In some years there are pamphlets published. Mr. Bell Dawson has been in charge of the service for a good many years.

part of the British Empire. From a point twenty miWs inland observations taken showed that the land' was mountainous, some of the peaks appearing fifty miles distant. Mr. ,H. BOULAY: (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I think, once before, last year, I called the attention of the Minister of Marine to the importance of establishing a life-saving station in the lower St. Lawrence. All along the coast from Gaspe to Rimouski, there is practically no boat that may be any help in a shipwreck occurring in that part of the river.
I am aware that at Rimouski the Eureka and the Lady Evelyn are often taken out to shipwrecks; but from Rimouski to Gaspe, there is no life-saving station.
While discussing this item, I recall stating last year that the dangers in the navigation of the St. Lawrence could be avoided by changing the system now followed in taking on and off pilots at Father Point. 1 often wonder why it is there are not more accidents occurring at that spot while the present system of taking pilots on and off the steamers is in force. In foggy weather, the steamers coming up know where they have to go at Father Point to get their pilots. Those that go down the river go the same way and reach as close to the shore as possible. In a deep fog, there could easily be a collision; that is how the disas-

ter to the Empress of Ireland was brought about.
I believe the system should be changed and pilots should not be taken on at the same point as where they are taken off. At Matane there is a splendid place for taking off pilots, while they could board the steamer at Father Point. Of course, to carry that out the dredging of the river at Matane would be required, as well as the building of a breakwater; but I believe that such a system would do away with any danger of accident.
I gave a good deal of thought to the matter, and I know that numerous accidents may happen oh account of the pilots being let off at the same place they are taken on. Of course, I know that in clear weather, the vessels can easily avoid one another; but in a fog, it is sometimes impossible to see far enough ahead to prevent collisions.
I suggest to the minister that he consider that question seriously. I am not a seaman and may be astray in my views, but I do certainly think that the subject is worthy of consideration.
I have been pointing out to the minister the desirability of a life saving station near Father Point, and of a change in the system of taking on and putting off the pilots in the St. Lawrerfce so as to avoid the danger of a collision. I hope the minister will give this matter his serious consideration after reading my remarks in Hansard to-morrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
While I was not -able to
follow my hon. friend as well as I should have liked, I shall have very great pleasure in reading his remarks in Hansard to-morrow. The matter of a life saving station near Father Point has been considered ,by the department, and the officials who are specially charged with the carrying on of this work say that during the season of navigation there are almost always two boats at Rimouski with steam up: the Eureka, a pilot boat, and the Lady Evelyn, which carries the mail to and from the trans-Atlantic steamers. These are both Government boats; their crews are paid by the Government, and are quite as efficient as any life s-aving crew. As these boats have steam up all the time my officials do not see the necessity of a life saving station at that point. I agree entirely with what my hon. friend says about the system of taking on and putting off the pilots. We have considered this matter before, and have come to the conclusion that a change
in the system is desirable. In order to carry out the system suggested by my hon. friend, we shall have to have a newer and more modern boat, and we were thinking of obtaining a boat of that sort just before war broke out. But as it would cost us between $180,000 and $200,000 we have hesitated about buying it under existing conditions. I entirely agree that the system suggested by my hon. friend would avoid the danger of collision by the boats crossing one another, and it is only because we do* not wish to embark on anything but absolutely necessary expenditures at this time that we have not purchased a boat and adopted the system.

Whan the minister's Estimates were up a few weeks ago he said he would see whether anything could be done to induce the. coal companies to give cargoes to small sailing, vessels. , If something of the sort is not done, -certain sections of the country which have not railway communication will be without coal this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Under present conditions, with the shortage of tonnage, small sailing vessels -should h-ave plenty of chances to get into the docks and take on a cargo of coal. I would suggest that, as the coal mines are owned by the Government of Nova S-cotia, they might be in a better position than we are to do something in this direction.
I

A similar condition,
though not -so acute, existed some years ago. I think it was Mr. Fielding who took the m-atter up with the coal companies, and for a few years after they did better, but the situation is again becoming acute; for instance, in the Magdalen Islands and certain portions of Prince Edward Island. There is always a slack period in the -summer months during which these sailing vessels would carry coal if they had not to wait two or three weeks at the docks to get a cargo.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I should think any vessel
could get a cargo now.

I was speaking of next
summer. Perhaps the minister could make some inquiries of the coal companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have done so. But
the difficulty is that the larger vessels get into the docks, and. the smaller vessels are kept waiting until they are loaded. I am told that at one time the Dominion Coal

Company built a dock for the accommodation of small vessels.
I was speaking of Pictou.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I was speaking of Sydney. I did not know there was the same difficulty at Pictou; but with the shortage of tonnage this year, I think small vessels should have no trouble in getting a cargo.

The trouble is that while the small vessels are waiting for a big steamer to leave the dock, another steameT comes in and then perhaps another, and the small vessels have to wait till they are all loaded.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Government cannot
control that sort of thing very well.
Except by advice.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think the only way would be to have a special dock for these small vessels. I understand the Dominion Coal Company provided that accommodation at one time.

Their coal is not generally used for domestic purposes, but the coal from Pictou and Inverness mines.
Naval Service-patrol of the Northern waters of Canada-further amount required, $35,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This amount is to provide for certain unforeseen expenditures in connection with the purchase of the Polar Bear, which cost $20,000, and the charter of the Polar Bear at one time at a cost of $4,000. It covers also provisions Mr. Stefansson had to purchase. This $35,000 will clean everything up.

Is the Polar Bear a new
boat?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not ;think it was a new boat. It had been in the whaling trade for some time before Stefansson bought it.	\
Has the minister a description of the vessel ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, 'but I am told that she is a staunch, strong vessel. The Karluk, hon. gentlemen willremember, was jammed in the ice and another vessel had to be purchased.

to provide for the expenses of investigating; claims for compensation under the Pelagic Sealing Treaty-further amount required, $4,100.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This winds up the cost of the pelagic sealing investigation. About

1,600 claims far damages were filed against the Government by people who had been engaged in the sealing business and who claimed that they were entitled to damages because of the treaty that was entered into a few years ago under which pelagic sealing was entirely abolished. Mr. Justice Audette, of the Exchequer Court, was appointed to hear the claims and report upon them. The amount of the claims filed aggregated	$9,200,000. Most	of the
claimants were represented by counsel, and the investigation was a very long one. Judge Audette had to hold court for lengthened periods at Victoria; once he went to Halifax, where there were a few claimants. In his report Judge Audette finds that $61,000, in round figures, should be paid to different claimants.
What is the total cost of this investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Somewhere in the neighbourhood of $30,000. An immense volume of evidence was taken, and the charges in that way were very high. We paid J udge Audette $40 for each day in which he was actually engaged in the work. On beihalf of the Government one counsel was employed to investigate these claims and to see that they were properly placed before the judge. I am told that no further amount will be required.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Supplementary Estimates that we have just passed were for the past year; those for the present year have not yet been brought down. As the hon. member for Guysborough has stated,
I was waited upon by a delegation composed of a number of leading citizens of Ottawa who were interested in this movement, and by a number of members of the House of Commons. Some information which I then asked for concerning the scope and work of the hospital has since been furnished me and I should like to say to my hon. friend that I am entirely in sympathy with the movement. The subscription asked for $5,000, is a moderate one, and I intend asking my colleagues to authorize me to include that amount in my Supplementary Estimates.
